questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define specific heat capacity. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Describe an experiment, to measure the specific heat capacity of a liquid. Include in your description:

- a diagram of the set-up
- the procedure
- data collected
- how the data will be used to obtain the specific heat capacity of the liquid
- any precaution you will take to minimize errors. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The **specific heat capacity** of a substance is the **quantity of heat (energy) needed to raise the temperature of $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ of the substance by $1\,\mathrm{K}$ ($1\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$)**: $c = \dfrac{Q}{m\,\Delta\theta}$. Unit: $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

(ii) **Electrical method with an immersion heater.**

**Apparatus:** a copper calorimeter with a stirrer and a lid, the liquid, an electric immersion heater, a d.c. power supply (or battery), an ammeter, a voltmeter, a switch, a thermometer ($-10$ to $110\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$), a stopwatch, a top-pan balance, lagging (cotton wool or felt) and a larger beaker or box to hold it, connecting wires.

**Diagram of the set-up (described):** the calorimeter, containing the liquid, stands inside the lagging. The immersion heater, completely covered by the liquid, the thermometer and the stirrer pass through holes in the lid. The heater is connected in **series** with the ammeter, the switch and the power supply, and the voltmeter is connected **in parallel** across the heater.

**Procedure:**

1. Measure the mass $m_c$ of the empty, dry calorimeter with the stirrer. Pour in enough liquid to cover the heater and measure the new mass: the mass of liquid is $m$.
2. Place the calorimeter in the lagging, insert the heater and the thermometer, stir, and read the initial temperature $\theta_1$.
3. Connect the circuit as described, switch on and start the stopwatch at the same instant. Read and record the voltage $V$ and the current $I$ (keep them constant by adjusting the supply if needed).
4. Stir gently all the time. After a time $t$ (for example 5 minutes) switch off and stop the clock; keep stirring and read the **highest** temperature reached, $\theta_2$.
5. Repeat for other times or masses and take the average of the values of $c$.

**Data collected:** $m_c$ (kg), $m$ (kg), $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ ($^\circ\mathrm{C}$), $V$ (V), $I$ (A), $t$ (s). Example of readings: $m_c = 0.10\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m = 0.20\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\theta_1 = 25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $\theta_2 = 40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $V = 12\,\mathrm{V}$, $I = 4\,\mathrm{A}$, $t = 300\,\mathrm{s}$.

**Use of the data:** the electrical energy supplied is $VIt$; it heats the liquid and the calorimeter (specific heat capacity of copper $c_c$, taken from tables):

$$VIt = m\,c\,(\theta_2-\theta_1) + m_c\,c_c\,(\theta_2-\theta_1)\quad\Rightarrow\quad c = \dfrac{VIt - m_c c_c(\theta_2-\theta_1)}{m\,(\theta_2-\theta_1)}$$

**Precautions:** lag the calorimeter and use the lid to reduce heat losses; stir continuously so that the temperature is uniform; keep the heater fully immersed and the thermometer bulb in the liquid without touching the heater or the walls; begin a few degrees below room temperature and stop a few degrees above it, so that the heat lost balances the heat gained from the surroundings; read the highest temperature after switching off; use a large enough temperature rise and repeat the experiment.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Differentiate between conduction and convection. *[2 marks]*

(ii) In the coastal town of Limbe, during the day, the breeze blows from the sea to the land. Briefly explain how this comes about. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Conduction** is the transfer of heat through a material (mainly a solid) by the vibration of its particles and the movement of free electrons, **without any movement of the material itself**. **Convection** is the transfer of heat in a **fluid (liquid or gas) by the movement of the fluid itself**: the warmer, less dense fluid rises and the cooler, denser fluid sinks, forming convection currents.

(ii) During the day the **land heats up faster than the sea** (the sea has a much larger specific heat capacity and mixes). The air above the land is heated, **expands, becomes less dense and rises**, leaving a region of lower pressure over the land. The cooler, denser air above the sea then **moves in over the land to take its place**: this is the **sea breeze**, a convection current (the warm air rising over the land flows back out to sea at height).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) What is a bimetallic strip? *[2 marks]*

(ii) Explain what happens to a bimetallic strip when it is heated? *[2 marks]*

(iii) Give one use or application of a bimetallic strip. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) A **bimetallic strip** consists of **two strips of different metals** (for example brass and iron) of the same length, **firmly joined (riveted or welded) together** along their length.

(ii) When heated, both metals expand, but they expand by **different amounts** (brass has a larger linear expansivity than iron). Because they are joined, the strip **bends into a curve**, with the metal that expands more (brass) on the **outside of the curve**. When it cools again it straightens (and bends the other way if cooled below its original temperature).

(iii) Use: in a **thermostat** (electric iron, oven, refrigerator) the strip bends and opens or closes the contacts to switch the heater off or on. (Other accepted uses: fire alarm, flasher unit of car indicators, circuit breaker.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) State Snell's law. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Describe an experiment to measure the refractive index of a glass block. Include in your description:

- a diagram of the set-up
- the procedure
- data collected
- how the data will be used to obtain the refractive index of the glass
- any precaution you will take to minimize errors. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Snell's law:** for a ray of light of a given colour passing from one medium into another, the **ratio $\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ is constant** ($i$ = angle of incidence, $r$ = angle of refraction, both measured from the normal). This constant is the refractive index $n$ of the second medium relative to the first.

(ii) **Pin method with a rectangular glass block.**

**Apparatus:** a rectangular glass block, a drawing board, a sheet of white paper, four optical pins, a protractor, a ruler, a sharp pencil, drawing pins (or tape).

**Diagram of the set-up (described):** the glass block lies on the sheet of paper pinned on the board; its outline $ABCD$ is drawn. The normal $NN'$ is drawn at a point $O$ on face $AB$; the incident ray is the line through pins $P_1$ and $P_2$ meeting $O$ at an angle $i$ to the normal; the emergent ray is seen through face $CD$ and fixed by pins $P_3$ and $P_4$; the refracted ray inside the block is the line $OO'$.

**Procedure:**

1. Place the block on the paper and draw its outline $ABCD$ with the pencil. Remove it, draw the normal at $O$ on $AB$, and draw a line through $O$ making an angle $i = 20^\circ$ with the normal.
2. Replace the block on its outline. Stick pins $P_1$ and $P_2$ upright on the incident line, at least $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ apart.
3. Looking through face $CD$, place pins $P_3$ and $P_4$ so that they appear exactly in line with the images of $P_1$ and $P_2$.
4. Remove the block and the pins. Draw the line through $P_3$ and $P_4$ to meet $CD$ at $O'$, and join $O$ to $O'$. Measure the angle of refraction $r$ between $OO'$ and the normal at $O$.
5. Repeat for $i = 30^\circ, 40^\circ, 50^\circ, 60^\circ$.

**Data collected:** a table of $i$, $r$, $\sin i$ and $\sin r$. Example: $i = 20^\circ, 30^\circ, 40^\circ, 50^\circ, 60^\circ$ with $r = 13^\circ, 19^\circ, 25^\circ, 31^\circ, 35^\circ$ (illustrative values).

**Use of the data:** calculate $n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ for each pair and take the average; or plot $\sin i$ (y-axis) against $\sin r$ (x-axis): the points lie on a **straight line through the origin whose gradient is the refractive index** $n$ of the glass (about 1.5).

**Precautions:** use a sharp pencil and fine lines; hold the pins vertical and place them far apart, to define the ray accurately; look at the bottom of the pins when lining them up; do not move the block or the paper during the experiment; avoid very small or very large angles of incidence; repeat for several angles and average.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define critical angle. *[2 marks]*

(ii) State two conditions necessary for total internal reflection to occur. *[2 marks]*

(iii) Name a device that makes use of total internal reflection. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The **critical angle** is the **angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the less dense medium is $90^\circ$** (the refracted ray travels along the boundary).

(ii) Total internal reflection occurs when: (1) light travels from a **denser medium to a less dense medium** (for example glass or water to air); (2) the **angle of incidence in the denser medium is greater than the critical angle**.

(iii) An **optical fibre** (also acceptable: a totally reflecting prism in a periscope or binoculars, an endoscope).

questions.enonce_markdown:
A guitar is an example of a string instrument.

(i) State two factors that affect the frequency of the string. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Explain how one of the factors named in f(i) can be varied on the guitar. *[2 marks]*

(iii) Give one other example of a string instrument. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The frequency of a vibrating string depends on (any two): its **length**, its **tension**, and its **mass per unit length** (thickness and material of the string).

(ii) **Tension:** turning the tuning peg tightens or loosens the string; a tighter string has a **higher tension and gives a higher frequency (higher pitch)**. (Or **length:** pressing the string against a fret with a finger shortens the vibrating length, so the frequency is **higher**.)

(iii) Another string instrument: a **violin** (also accepted: cello, harp, banjo, piano, sonometer).
